p: Wednesday, January 5, Maria opened a blank document and typed: Cascade Valley Health, Information Technology Strategic Plan, 2028 to 2030. Then she stopped.

The last one was in the shared drive. Ochoa had written it three years ago, 2025 to 2027, forty pages with his name on the cover. She read it at her desk with a cup of coffee going cold. Every initiative had a date beside it, and nearly every date had a check mark. MedaLink was on page thirty-one, in one line: assess options before end of support. Somebody had done that. It had taken her fifteen months.
She'd never written a CIO's plan. She'd never been in the room when one was written. And the board would read this one as Ochoa's, whoever typed it.

That afternoon she went down the hall to ask him where to start. His door was open and his chair was empty. The bookshelf behind his desk had gaps in it. Marcus had come up from the basement that morning carrying an interface engine manual from 1998. Ochoa had given it to him, and Marcus said it was wrong about everything and he was keeping it anyway.
Her phone buzzed on the walk back. Lucia. med surg starts monday. hospital, real patients. what do i bring
Maria typed the first true thing she thought of. Two pens that work. A watch with a second hand. Eat before you go. A minute later: that's it? That's most of it.

Back at her desk she wrote one question under the title, the one Ochoa had asked her in April about the business case. Who reads this in 2030? Then she sat looking at it for a long time, because she didn't know.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: the last page.
Sunday, January 9, Ochoa took the back booth at the Greeley diner and pushed the legal pad across the table to her side, pen and all. You write this time, he said. I'll talk.

Strategic planning starts above IT. The organization has a mission, why it exists, and a vision, where it wants to be. Before it sets goals, it scans its environment with a SWOT: strengths and weaknesses inside, opportunities and threats outside, like payers, regulation, the workforce, and attackers. Then it sets a few goals for three to five years. The IT strategic plan comes after, and it traces back to those goals one by one. That's strategic alignment. A project that can't name the goal it serves doesn't go in.

The plan itself has a shape. Where you are: a current state assessment of applications, infrastructure, people, spending, and risks. Where the organization's going. The initiatives that close the gap, on a roadmap by year. How decisions get made, which is governance. What it costs, capital and operating. How you'll know it worked, which is measures. And what could go wrong. It serves every kind of place the system runs: hospitals, a critical access hospital, clinics, home health, and any partner you host, like a community health center with its own board and its own patients.

How the exam asks it. The IT plan derives from the organization's strategic plan, not from IT's backlog or a vendor's roadmap. What comes first is the organization's goals and a current state assessment. Strategic alignment means naming the goal each initiative serves.
Everybody will want something in it, Ochoa said. Your job is to say what fits, and show why.

Forecast first, from drivers: patient volumes, new services, users, and the plan's own initiatives, redone every year. Then manage everything as one portfolio, because every project draws on the same people and the same money. Mandatory work goes first: security, regulation, and anything losing vendor support. Rank the rest against the goals, risk, and value, and against capacity in analyst hours, not just dollars. Draw the line. Above it is funded and staffed. Below it gets a date or an honest no.

Each initiative comes in as a proposal with a benefits realization plan: an owner in the business, a baseline, a target, and review dates. Then show your work. Put the resources, the budget, and the ranking where a hospital president can see why her request sits below the line, and what would move it up.

How the exam asks it. For competing requests, the answer is governance that ranks by strategic criteria and capacity, then publishes the result with reasons. To promote stakeholder understanding, show the resources, the budget, and where each request sits, openly.

A key performance indicator, a KPI, is a measure tied to a goal, with a target, an owner, a data source, and a schedule. A service level agreement sets performance targets between a provider and its customer, inside the organization or out. A vendor SLA usually adds remedies. KPIs often measure SLAs. Pick a few of each.

Comparative analytics holds you against others. A benchmark is only fair if the definitions match and the peers look like you. Report where you fall, median or percentile, and treat the gap as a question to answer.

Then the money. Operating budgets pay for this year: salaries, subscriptions, support. Capital buys things that last. Budget variance is budget minus actual. For an expense line, a negative variance is unfavorable. Divide by the budget for the percent. Split one-time causes from recurring ones, and reforecast. Glenn forgives a bad month, Ochoa said. He doesn't forgive a surprise.

How the exam asks it. Expect a variance calculation and a benchmark trap: check definitions and the peer group before acting on a gap. Judge a predictive model or a pilot on your own data, by site, against a matched baseline. An area under the curve of 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect.

People are most of the plan, he said. And the part nobody writes down. A job description names a role's purpose, its duties, its decision rights, who it reports to, and the skills it needs. Write what the role doesn't own, too. For any role one person holds alone, write a succession plan: who could step in, how ready they are, and what training gets them there.

New roles belong in the plan when the work has outgrown the old ones. A chief nursing information officer leads nursing informatics the way the CMIO leads it for physicians. Policies carry the plan's rules. A policy says what and why, and governance approves it. A procedure says how. Each needs an owner and a review date.

How the exam asks it. For a single point of failure in a person, the answer is a written succession plan with named, trained backups, not a quick hire or an informal promise. Policies need governance approval and an owner, not an email.

When two leaders both look at you in a meeting, don't pick a side. Name what they agree on, settle the criteria before the options, and decide by the method the room agreed to. In a board meeting the chair runs the room, and when the chair hands you the floor, the same rules hold. In front of a board, lead with the recommendation and the decision you need, show the risks, and brief the people who'll speak before the meeting starts.
How the exam asks it. In a conflict, the facilitator's first move is common ground and criteria, not a vote or a side. For a board, the recommendation comes first.

Ochoa paid, then sat back down. One more. This field changes faster than a nursing license does. Keeping IT competencies current means continuing education, professional associations, conferences, and certifications that make you keep learning to renew them. For the team, it means a development plan for each person, with time and money behind it. Kiran has a CPHIMS study guide in his drawer. Marcus told him to get one. Fund what they ask for.
Maria had brought something too. It had come Saturday, in Irene's square handwriting, a card with a wren on the front. She slid it across the table.

A card from Irene Kowalski. Santos. You told me Sunday that Ray handed you his plan to write. Ray doesn't hand anybody anything by accident. Write it for the night shift. They're the ones who find out if it works. I renewed my critical care certification every three years until I retired, and every time I learned what I'd forgotten. Keep learning, and make your people do it too. Coffee's still bad. Come by. I.K.

Ochoa read it. He folded it along its crease and handed it back without a word about the second line. Irene Kowalski, he said. She always did read a room before she walked into it. Then he tore off the page Maria had filled and gave her that too.
How the exam asks it. To maintain competencies, choose ongoing education, certification with renewal requirements, and funded development plans over one-time training at go-live.

Monday, January 10, Maria had two days and nine pages. Kiran had sent her a spreadsheet of every open request from every hospital, forty-four rows. Corvane had sent its product roadmap for the next three years, with a cover note from Brett. Aisha had sent a list titled What We Should Be Doing, and it was good.

Ochoa's old plan sat open in the other window. Three sources, and all of them were somebody's list. She could see a plan that was mostly a long table of projects with prices beside them. It would be done by Friday.
A. Start from the system's goals and a current state check, then fit the work.
B. Build it on Corvane's three-year roadmap, since the EHR is most of what IT runs.
C. Update Ochoa's 2025 plan with new dates, since its structure already worked.
D. Turn Kiran's forty-four requests into a three-year schedule, with costs and dates.

She pulls Cascade's strategic plan, five goals, and writes each across the top of a page. Then a current state assessment, one page per area: applications, infrastructure, people, spending, risks. Rawlins is in it twice, once for the network and once for the locks. Only then does she open Kiran's spreadsheet, and each of his forty-four rows gets the goal it serves, or a blank. Eleven rows stay blank. Kiran reads them and laughs a little. Four of those are mine.

That's the move. An IT strategic plan derives from the organization's strategy. Start with the goals and a current state assessment, then fill in initiatives, a roadmap, governance, costs, measures, and risks. Requests that can't name a goal get questioned.

Thursday, January 13, the chief executive of Snowy Range Community Health called from Laramie. Her health center wasn't part of Cascade. It ran six clinics in two counties, saw anyone who walked in, and charged on a sliding scale by income. About a third of its patients had no insurance. Its old EHR vendor had just been bought, and the price had doubled.
Half our patients end up at your hospitals, she said. We'd like to come onto your Corvane. Corvane says big customers can host small ones. Could you put us in your plan?
Kiran was already thinking about the build. We have forty clinics on Corvane. It'd be forty-six. Same build.
A. Plan it as its own organization, with a hosting agreement, a BAA, and its own needs.
B. Treat Snowy Range as six more Cascade clinics, using the same build and policies.
C. Decline, since Snowy Range isn't Cascade and its patients aren't Cascade's job.
D. Add it to year three, and work out the details once One Chart has settled.

Maria puts it in the plan's second year as a hosted partner, with its own line. A hosting agreement and a business associate agreement, written with Joan. Its own records and access, walled off from Cascade's except where a patient's care crosses over. Sliding fee billing and its federal grant reports in the build. A seat at the clinical informatics council. The chief executive reads the draft and says it's the first time a hospital system asked what her patients needed instead of what her clinics cost.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Know the type of organization. A community health center serves patients regardless of ability to pay, often on a sliding fee scale, with its own board and federal funding rules. Hosting it means a separate organization with its own agreements, privacy boundaries, and needs.

Tuesday, January 18, the three Wyoming CNOs and the system's chief nursing officer read the people section of Maria's draft. Gail had circled one line in pencil. Nursing informatics: covered by the vice president of clinical systems.

That's you, Gail said. You've been our nursing informatics officer for fifteen months, and it isn't anybody's job. Aisha has a title for the doctors. We don't. She let that sit. Denise Harmon asked me last week whether anybody was ever going to write that job.
A. Make it an IT director post in clinical systems that builds nursing content.
B. Create a CNIO: a nurse leader who owns nursing informatics, peer to the CMIO.
C. Keep nursing informatics with clinical systems, and revisit it after year one.
D. Fold nursing into Aisha's role, so one leader owns all clinical informatics.

She writes it into the plan's first year. A chief nursing information officer, reporting to the system CNO with a dotted line to the CIO. Co-chair of the council with Aisha. Owns nursing documentation, BCMA practice, and nurse adoption. She wrote it knowing it was the part of the job she'd miss, which was how she knew it had to be somebody's whole job. IT builds what that role and the council decide. Gail reads it and taps the dotted line. That's the part that makes it real.

Exactly right. Know the HIMS roles. The CNIO leads nursing informatics the way the CMIO leads it for physicians: nursing's voice in design, content, and adoption. IT is the builder. Write the role so it doesn't depend on who's in it now.
Thursday, January 20, Glenn's year-end report came in at 7:02, the way his emails always did.

An email from Glenn Morrow. Subject: Clinical systems, 2027. Maria, your 2027 operating budget was $18.4 million. Actual was $19.55 million. The board's finance committee will see this line in February, the same month it sees your plan. I'd like to understand it before they do. Glenn
He'd added a line under his name. Your business case held. Let's see if your budget did.

Kiran had the drivers by noon. Go-live overtime and superuser backfill, $820,000. The ransomware response and the insurance deductible, $250,000. The second Rawlins circuit, started early, $180,000 for the year. MedaLink support ended a month early, which saved $100,000.
A. Cover the overrun by quietly deferring a 2028 project, so the total looks right.
B. Show each driver, split one-time from recurring, and reforecast 2028.
C. Report the total, and explain that it was all from go-live, which is over.
D. Point out the overrun came from vendor and insurer costs outside her control.

One page. The total, 6.25 percent over. Then each driver, marked one-time or recurring. The go-live, the ransomware, and MedaLink's early end were one-time, $970,000 net. The circuit recurs, $180,000 a year that the 2028 budget never had. She adds it to the 2028 reforecast with a line about why. Glenn reads it at his desk. So what recurs is a hundred and eighty thousand. And it's in next year's budget now.

That's the move. Explain a variance by its drivers. Budget minus actual gives the size. Splitting one-time from recurring tells finance what will happen again, and the reforecast puts recurring costs where they belong. No surprises.

Tuesday, January 25, the forty-four requests came to the IT steering committee. Together they needed about 61,000 analyst hours over three years. After support and upgrades, Maria's team had about 38,000.

Each hospital president had sent one email about their own request. The Fort Collins president had sent two. Aisha's predictive program was on the list, and so was Nate's security work from Rawlins, and so was Snowy Range.
A. Take the ten biggest requests by cost, since those matter most to the board.
B. Fund the mandatory items, then let each hospital pick one of its own requests.
C. Put all forty-four requests in the plan, spread evenly across the three years.
D. Rank all forty-four in steering by goal, risk, and hours, then publish it.

Mandatory work goes first: Nate's security list and two regulatory changes. The rest get scored against the five goals, risk, and value, then stacked against the 38,000 hours. Twenty-six land above the line. Eighteen land below it, each with a date to come back or a plain no and the reason. Maria sends every hospital president the whole list, not just their own row. The Fort Collins president calls, annoyed. Then he asks what would move his request up, and she tells him.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Manage projects as one portfolio, and make it understandable. Put mandatory work first, rank the rest against strategy, risk, and value, and fit them to real capacity. Then publish the whole ranking, the hours, and the reasons, so every leader can see where they stand and what would change it.

Thursday, February 3, two days after Maria sent Ochoa her draft, Glenn's analyst brought a benchmark. A national survey of health systems put IT operating spending at a median of 3.1 percent of revenue. Cascade spent $46.8 million on $1.8 billion, 2.6 percent.
Aisha saw it before lunch. Put it on page one, she wrote. We're nine million under our peers. That pays for my whole program.
Tasha had sent one too. The service desk fixed 70 percent of calls on the first contact. The survey's median was 78.
A. Use the gap to ask the board for $9 million, since peers spend that much more.
B. Show it on page one, with a footnote saying definitions may differ.
C. Leave benchmarks out, since no two health systems are really alike.
D. Check its definitions and peers first, then use it beside outcomes.

Glenn's analyst rebuilds the peer group: multi-hospital systems with rural sites and no medical school, on the same definition of IT spending. The median drops to 2.8. Cascade is 0.2 points under, not 0.5. Tasha checks the desk number the same way. The survey counts password resets the phone system fixes on its own, and Cascade doesn't. Matched, the desk median is 74, so Cascade's 70 is a real gap, just a smaller one. The plan shows both gaps with their definitions, beside the outcomes. Aisha sighs. Three and a half million is still three and a half million. And Glenn will believe it.

Exactly right. Comparative analytics only works when definitions match and peers are truly comparable. Check both, report where you fall, and treat the gap as a question to explain, next to outcomes, before you use it to argue for money.

Tuesday, February 8, Aisha brought the Sepsis Predict results to Maria's office. Corvane's model had run silently since the April upgrade at the eight Corvane hospitals, and since October in Wyoming, scoring every patient and showing no one.

Corvane's brochure said its area under the curve was 0.87. Kiran had checked it against the residents' chart reviews, hospital by hospital. Greeley, 0.85. Fort Collins, 0.83. Cheyenne, 0.79. Rawlins, 0.68, on nineteen septic patients since October.
Overall it's 0.81, Aisha said. I want it live in all eleven on April first. It's the first thing in my section of the plan.
A. Keep it silent at all eleven until every site has a full year of data.
B. Use Corvane's 0.87 and its default threshold, since it's the vendor's model.
C. Go live where it's proven, keep it silent elsewhere, and recheck by site.
D. Turn it on everywhere April first, since 0.81 overall is a strong model.

Greeley and Fort Collins go live in April, with a threshold Kiran and Aisha pick from Cascade's own two by two. Cheyenne stays silent until it has more cases. Rawlins stays silent, and Aisha reads the nineteen charts to find out why. Every quarter, a named owner checks it by site. Aisha takes the plan line back and rewrites it herself. Two sites, then earn the rest.

That's the move. Interpret a predictive model on local data, site by site. Go live where it performs, set thresholds from your own results, keep it silent where it doesn't, and monitor for drift with an owner.

Monday, February 14, Joan called at 8:40. A first-year resident had asked her, politely, whether it was all right to paste patient notes into a free AI chatbot on his phone to draft discharge summaries. He'd been doing it for a month. So had three other residents.
He asked, Joan said. That's the good news. We have no policy that says no, and nothing in your plan that says what yes looks like.
Nate was on the line too. Penwright's AI is approved, with a BAA, he said. This one isn't. They can't tell the difference from the screen.
A. Email every clinician today that AI tools are banned, and call that the policy.
B. Have Nate block AI websites at the firewall, and leave it at that.
C. Let each department write its own AI rules, since the uses all differ.
D. Let Joan assess it, and take an AI policy through governance with an owner.

Before noon, Aisha tells the four residents to stop today, and why. Joan runs her assessment on their month. Maria drafts the policy with Joan, Nate, Aisha, and legal. Approved AI tools only, each with a BAA. No patient information in public ones. New AI tools come through the technology intake. Training for every clinician, an owner, and a review in a year. It goes to the policy committee in March, and into the plan as its own line. The resident who asked helps write the training.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Contain first: the disclosures stop today. Then policies need governance: an owner, the right approvers, a findable home, training, and a review date. A privacy event goes to the privacy officer. A good policy also names the safe option, so people don't need a workaround.

Thursday, February 17, Maria wrote Kiran's job down. The plan needed it. Every year of the roadmap leaned on the same two things: clinical content that stayed current, and superusers who could teach. Kiran had been doing both since October, on top of everything else, and nobody had written any of it down.

Halfway down the page she stopped at the line for skills. Year two brought Meadowlark's patch data and other outside tools into the chart through FHIR. Years two and three took Sepsis Predict to the other hospitals, and after Monday's call about the residents and the chatbot, somebody had to be able to judge every AI tool that came in. The last class anyone on her team had taken was Corvane's build training for One Chart. Most of what they knew about FHIR, they'd learned from Marcus at a whiteboard.

She asked Kiran to her office at four, so he'd have to leave at five. He came in with a notebook, as if it were a meeting about somebody else. When she showed him the skills line, he nodded. I've been reading about the sepsis model at night, he said. I can keep up.
A. Encourage study on their own time, and pay back any certification they pass.
B. Map the plan's skills to each role, find the gaps, and fund a plan per person.
C. Bring in contractors who already know the new tools as each project gets started.
D. Send Kiran and two of the analysts to Corvane's user conference every single year.

They build it together before five. Maria lists what the plan needs by year: FHIR apps, model validation, AI tool review, and the content work. Kiran rates himself and the team against it, honestly, on his third try. Each person gets a development plan with four protected hours a week on the schedule, a paid certification where the role needs one, and a review every January. Not at night, Maria says. Tuesday afternoons, on the schedule, where I can see it. Then the role page itself. Clinical content and superuser program lead. He runs the council's content process and the train the trainer program. He doesn't own clinical content, the clinicians do. He isn't on call; the team rotates. Yesenia, the analyst Marcus taught first, is his deputy, and she shadows him on content until she can cover it. The skills the role keeps current are on the page, with the hours to learn them. Kiran reads to the bottom. You wrote my hours into a job description. Somebody had to.

Exactly right. Maintaining competencies starts from the strategy. Name the skills the plan will need, assess each person against them, and fund a development plan with protected time, certification where it matters, cross-training, and a yearly review. Learning that only happens at go-live or after midnight doesn't keep a team current.

Tuesday, February 22, Marcus came up from the basement at seven with a binder under his arm. Four inches thick, tabbed in three colors, RELAY on the spine in his block capitals. He set it on Maria's desk.
He sat down without being asked, which he did now. Good binder, he said. It was what he'd said about the one in Omaha.

Then he told her. His granddaughter in Tucson had a brother now. He wanted four days a week starting in July, and to be done for good at the end of 2030. Your plan says Relay runs through 2030, he said. Somebody has to run it after. I want it in writing who. And I want it in writing that I'm here till I say I'm not.
A. Write a plan with him: two named successors, skill dates, and his role to 2030.
B. Keep it informal, since he's earned her trust and a plan would feel cold.
C. Post his job now, so a new engineer can shadow him before July.
D. Name the analyst he trained as his successor, and give her Relay in July.

They write it together that morning. Two named successors: the other analyst he's been teaching, and a second he picks himself. Every Relay skill in his binder gets a sign-off date for each of them, the hardest last. From July he's principal interface engineer, four days a week, teaching, through December 2030, and the last line says the date moves only if he moves it. Maria signs it. Marcus reads the last line again. This in my file? It's in the plan.

That's the move. For a critical role held by one person, write a succession plan: named successors, readiness for each skill, training to close the gaps, and the incumbent's role in writing. Build it with the person, so passing on what he knows is his job, not his exit.
Tuesday, March 7, at 7:30, Ochoa didn't have a legal pad. He had her plan, eighty pages, with his initials on every one.
I'm retiring, he said. March thirty-first. I told the board chair in July. On Friday I'm going to tell the rest of them, and I'm going to recommend you as interim CIO. They'll decide. Not me.

Maria didn't say anything for a while. She thought about the go or no-go meeting, and the command center in Cheyenne, and the exit conference at Greeley a year and a half ago. Every time, he'd taken a chair along the wall. You sat along the wall all year, she said.
I told you I'd be furniture, he said. I didn't say it was practice. Then, plainer: If I'd told you in October, you'd have run go-live for me. You ran it for Rawlins. I needed to know you would.

Irene told me in January, Maria said. I didn't hear it. That's what Irene's for. She looked at his initials, one on every page. Who do I call at two in the morning? Nobody. You built it so nobody has to.

Wednesday she drove to Greeley to see Bev's pilot before Friday. The remote station sat at the charge desk on the fourth floor, where the fax machine used to be: two screens, two Rawlins beds, a headset. Bev was in the chair. Kid. You look like you're about to take report. Ochoa's retiring. Bev slid the headset down around her neck and looked at her a long moment. Then take it.

Gail wanted Bev's numbers in Friday's plan. Five weeks, twenty-six patients watched. Five went to Greeley. In the same five weeks last year, twelve of twenty-nine similar patients had made the three-hour ride. Transfers cut by more than half, Gail had written. Put that on the slide.
A. Leave the pilot out of the plan, since five weeks can't show anything yet.
B. Report only the transfers avoided, seven patients kept at home in five weeks.
C. Show counts beside last year's, call it early, and judge it at six months.
D. Put Gail's line on the slide, since the drop from 41 percent to 19 is large.

The slide says five of twenty-six this year, twelve of twenty-nine last year, five weeks in, too early to call. Beside it are the balancing measures. One patient kept at Rawlins had to transfer the next morning. Nights at both units are surveyed too. The six-month review date sits at the bottom. Bev reads it over her shoulder. That's how I'd chart it. Gail, on the phone, says fine, and that she'll say promising.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Interpret small-number outcomes honestly. Show counts, not just percents, against a matched baseline. Say it's early, add balancing measures for the risks, and judge it at the review the pilot set in advance.

Friday, March 10, the board met at two on the sixth floor. Ochoa spoke first, for four minutes. He was retiring at the end of the month. He recommended Maria Santos as interim CIO, and the board would take it up in executive session after the plan. Then he went and sat along the wall.
Maria led with the ask: approve the plan, and $3.0 million in new capital for its first year. Twenty minutes in, she reached the capital page, and the room split.

Patients die of sepsis, not firewalls, Aisha said. She wanted $2.2 million: Sepsis Predict, Bev's remote ICU at Laramie, and Meadowlark for four hundred patients. A clinic in Rawlins was closed for a week, Glenn said. He wanted $2.4 million for Nate's security list first. Together that was $4.6 million. Every face at the table turned to Maria.
A. Ask the board to send the capital question to its finance committee next month.
B. Split the $3.0 million evenly between Aisha's programs and Glenn's list.
C. Name the shared goal, agree on criteria, then stage the money behind gates.
D. Back Glenn's security list, since the ransomware is the board's freshest worry.

You're both talking about the same thing, she says. The night nobody's watching. Then she asks them for the criteria, not the money: harm prevented, how sure we are, and when we'd know. Both write theirs on the same page. Measured that way, the plan is $1.6 million for the security items Nate rates high, now. $0.2 million to take Sepsis Predict live at Greeley and Fort Collins. $1.2 million for the remote ICU and Meadowlark, released in September if the pilots meet the measures they set in advance. Glenn checks the sum. Aisha checks the gate. The board votes yes.

Exactly right. Present a recommendation the board can test. Start from the shared goal, agree on the criteria before the options, and show how the money follows the evidence. Staged funding with gates lets data settle what argument can't, and the board decides on the merits, not on who argued louder.
The board went into executive session at 3:40. Maria waited in the hallway outside with Aisha and Glenn, the three of them standing by the window with nothing to do, which none of them was good at.

September, Aisha said finally. If Bev's numbers hold, I get my money. If they hold, Glenn said. I wrote the gate. I'll be the first one to open it. Aisha looked at him like she was deciding whether that was a joke. It wasn't, and she seemed to like that better.

At 4:15 the board chair came out. The board had named Maria Santos interim chief information officer, starting Monday, April 3. Interim, he said. For a year. After the year at Rawlins, the audit committee will want to see what you do with security and privacy. Then we'll talk about the rest. He shook her hand. Ray says you'll tell us the truth early. Do that.
Ochoa walked her to her car, the way he had in Greeley the day the survey ended. Sundays, he said. Seven thirty. Bring the legal pad. I'll still make you write. Who pays? The one with the job.

The next week the board secretary sent the conflict of interest form every officer signs. Under gifts from vendors in the last two years, Maria wrote none, and attached Pam's log, which said declined and disclosed, April 2027. It was the easiest page in the stack.
She called Irene from the car. Interim, she said. For a year. Did you write it for the night shift?
I tried. Then they'll tell you.
Friday, March 31, Ochoa's last day, there was no party. He'd said no to one. At five he walked out the front door with one box, like anybody else.
Maria Santos had been the interim CIO for forty minutes when the letter arrived.

The office was at the far end of the fourth floor hall. The nameplate still said the last person's name. On the windowsill was a small jade plant that hadn't been there before, with an index card in front of it in Ochoa's handwriting. Water it every other Sunday. R.O.
The letter had come in an envelope, handwritten, addressed to the CIO, and the mailroom had sent it up.

Letter from a Rawlins night nurse. Dear Ms. Santos,. I've been a night nurse on the medical floor in Rawlins for nineteen years. Somebody told me you worked nights in Greeley, so you'll know what I mean. For most of those years, at three in the morning, I was the only one awake who could check anything. Last Tuesday a man on my floor went bad at ten after three. A nurse in Greeley saw his pressure drop on her screen and called me before the monitor alarmed.
